paras: The threatened lynching of Cleve Toles and John Calvin took place at Luverne, Alabama, on August 28, 1910, when a crowd reported at more than 300 men gathered to go to Troy and lynch two Black men accused of an attempted assault on a white woman, Clair Fonville. Officials moved the prisoners by automobile from Troy to the Montgomery County jail before the crowd could reach them, and three weeks later both were convicted in the Crenshaw County circuit court and sentenced to twenty years.

J. C. Fonville of Luverne was preparing to move to his country home and had hired two Black draymen to haul his belongings to the depot. According to the Montgomery Advertiser's Luverne correspondent, a man entered Clair Fonville's room through a window a few minutes after midnight on Saturday, August 27, passed his hand over her face and grasped her arms, then fled when she and her mother screamed. Her brother Clifton, visiting from Montgomery, came to the room, and a posse soon arrested the two draymen, whom the paper named Cleveland Towles and John Carr.

Fearing mob violence, Crenshaw County Sheriff W. L. Tatum drove the two men to the Pike County jail at Troy on Sunday morning, a trip of an hour and a half. By 8 o'clock that evening, the Birmingham Age-Herald reported, over 300 men were in the street with plans to reach Troy about 2 a.m. Telephone contact with Luverne was lost after 8 o'clock, which the Age-Herald attributed to the mob closing the telephone office.

On learning that a mob was forming to lynch the prisoners, John D. McNeel, private secretary to the absent Governor Comer, ordered Pike County Sheriff W. C. Carroll to bring them to Montgomery. Carroll reached the Montgomery jail at 12:15 a.m. Monday and said he had been told a mob was already headed for Troy.

Two other Black men whom the prisoners had named, Fate Walker and Will Earl Mitchell, were "put through a sweat" in the Luverne guard house and released after witnesses placed them in Brantley. The same report said that Wilks Franklin, a Black man who had offered to guard the prisoners if given a gun, jumped from a railroad bridge and showed a hand apparently struck by a pistol ball; it did not say who fired.

The Fonville relatives let it be known that they wanted the law to take its course, "but will insist that there be no delay." The Crenshaw County grand jury took up the case on the first day of the term, indicted both men on Tuesday, September 13, and they were tried on Thursday evening. John Calvin, without counsel, questioned witnesses and offered an alibi, while Cleve Toles had a lawyer; each trial ended in a guilty verdict and the maximum sentence of twenty years.

All of the coverage found came from white papers; no Black-press report of the episode was found. The Montgomery Advertiser followed the case from arrest to sentence, crediting the sheriff's "prompt action" with preventing violence and ending its trial report with the remark that local feeling "only needs a leader to convene Judge Lynch's court."

A wire story ran on August 29 in the Washington Evening Star and the Richmond Times Dispatch, whose headline "Rush Prisoners to Safety" was paired with a subhead calling the men "Criminals." South Carolina papers carried a shorter version as "Jailed in Style" and "Taken to Jail in Style," describing Fonville as "a young white girl." A boilerplate item headed "May Lynch Negroes" appeared in Ohio and Kentucky weeklies on September 1, saying the prisoners had been sent away "to escape vengeance that seemed unavoidable."

The accused were named Cleveland Towles and John Carr, later Cleve Toles and John Calvin, in the Advertiser; Cleveland Coles and John Coldin in the wire; and John Colvin and Cleve Stowe in the Age-Herald. The local Advertiser, which followed the case to trial, is the stronger source for the names. The boilerplate version said the mob of 300 "left Luverne" and "marched 20 miles to Troy," while earlier and closer reports said only that it was forming or planning to move.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Cleve Toles and John Calvin
bases: A crowd gathered at Luverne to go to Troy and lynch two jailed Black men accused of an attempted assault, and officials moved them to Montgomery to prevent it (A2, A3, A4).

A crowd of over 300 men was reported gathering to take and lynch the two accused men for an alleged attempted assault (A3, A4, A6), but the prisoners were moved to Montgomery and no one was killed; they were later tried and sentenced in court (A2, A16).

The Montgomery Advertiser's Luverne special (A2), the Age-Herald's Montgomery special (A3) and the Associated Press-style wire (A4) independently report the arrests, the removal to Troy and Montgomery and the forming mob, though they differ on names.

accounts.label: Montgomery Advertiser Luverne correspondent
accounts.gist: A man entered through a window, passed his hand over Miss Fonville's face and bruised her arms before fleeing at the screams; two draymen were arrested on track and statement evidence and only the sheriff's 'prompt action' prevented mob violence.

accounts.label: Age-Herald Montgomery special
accounts.gist: Over 300 men gathered at Luverne by 8 p.m. planning to reach Troy at 2 a.m. and 'wreak the wrath of the people' on Colvin and Stowe; the telephone office was presumed closed by the mob.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Sheriff Tatum rushed Cleveland Coles and John Coldin to Troy, and McNeel ordered them to Montgomery on learning a mob was forming to lynch them.

accounts.label: Boilerplate wire
accounts.gist: A mob of 300 left Luverne and marched 20 miles to Troy declaring it would lynch Colvin and Stowe.

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser credited the sheriff's 'prompt action' with preventing mob violence, called the suspects 'negroes' and reported the evidence against them as a case; after the trial it wrote that feeling 'only needs a leader to convene Judge Lynch's court'.

Out-of-state papers ran the wire under headlines about the prisoners' safety or the automobile ('Rush Prisoners to Safety', 'Jailed in Style', 'Taken to Jail in Style'), with the Richmond paper calling them 'Criminals' in its subhead.
A boilerplate version ran as 'May Lynch Negroes' in Ohio and Kentucky weeklies, saying the prisoners were sent away 'to escape vengeance that seemed unavoidable'.
